entries.b7c4e225e83998dc6f994f81166845091b9346b7: <div sID="gen34235" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="19" osisID="Rev.19" sID="Rev.19"/> <div eID="gen34235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34236" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34237" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. A further account of the triumphant song of angels and saints for the fall of Babylon, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.1-Rev.19.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. The marriage between Christ and the church proclaimed and perfected, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.5-Rev.19.10">ver. 5-10</reference>. III. Another warlike expedition of the glorious head and husband of the church, with the success of it, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.10-Rev.19.21">ver. 10</reference>, &c.
entries.3777204f01e46473f123a15df6ecdc8fa19fd45c: <div eID="gen34237" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34236" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Triumph of the Saints. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 95.)</title> <div sID="gen34238" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And after these things I heard a great voice of much people in heaven, saying, Alleluia; Salvation, and glory, and honour, and power, unto the Lord our God: <hi type="super">2</hi> For true and righteous <hi type="italic">are</hi> his judgments: for he hath judged the great whore, which did corrupt the earth with her fornication, and hath avenged the blood of his servants at her hand. <hi type="super">3</hi> And again they said, Alleluia. And her smoke rose up for ever and ever. 4 And the four and twenty elders and the four beasts fell down and worshipped God that sat on the throne, saying, Amen; Alleluia. <div eID="gen34238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34239" type="x-p"/> The fall of Babylon being fixed, finished, and declared to be irrecoverable in the foregoing chapter, this begins with a holy triumph over her, in pursuance of the order given forth: <hi type="italic">Rejoice over her, thou heaven, and you holy apostles and prophets,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.18.20">ch. xviii. 20</reference>. They now gladly answer the call; and here you have, 1. The form of their thanksgiving, in that heavenly and most comprehensive word, <hi type="italic">Alleluia, praise you the Lord:</hi> with this they begin, with this they go on, and with this they end (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.4">v. 4</reference>); their prayers are now turned into praises, their hosannas end in halleluias. 2. The matter of their thanksgiving: they praise him for the truth of his word, and the righteousness of his providential conduct, especially in this great event—the ruin of Babylon, which had been a mother, nurse, and nest of idolatry, lewdness, and cruelty (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.2">v. 2</reference>), for which signal example of divine justice they ascribe <hi type="italic">salvation, and glory, and honour, and power, unto our God.</hi> 3. The effect of these their praises: when the angels and saints cried <hi type="italic">Alleluia,</hi> her fire burned more fiercely and <hi type="italic">her smoke ascended for ever and ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.19.3">v. 3</reference>. The surest way to have our deliverances continued and completed is to give God the glory of what he has done for us. Praising God for what we have is praying in the most effectual manner for what is yet further to be done for us; the praises of the saints blow up the fire of God's wrath against the common enemy. 4. The blessed harmony between the angels and the saints in this triumphant song, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.4">v. 4</reference>. The churches and their ministers take the melodious sound from the angels, and repeat it; falling down, and worshipping God, they cry, <hi type="italic">Amen, Alleluia.</hi>
entries.41305397009c10efe260d73a0d2492b4d5f747ad: <div eID="gen34239" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Triumph of the Saints. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 95.)</title> <div sID="gen34240" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> And a voice came out of the throne, saying, Praise our God, all ye his servants, and ye that fear him, both small and great. <hi type="super">6</hi> And I heard as it were the voice of a great multitude, and as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of mighty thunderings, saying, Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth. <hi type="super">7</hi> Let us be glad and rejoice, and give honour to him: for the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready. <hi type="super">8</hi> And to her was granted that she should be arrayed in fine linen, clean and white: for the fine linen is the righteousness of saints. <hi type="super">9</hi> And he saith unto me, Write, Blessed <hi type="italic">are</hi> they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb. And he saith unto me, These are the true sayings of God. <hi type="super">10</hi> And I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said unto me, See <hi type="italic">thou do it</hi> not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus: worship God: for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy. <div eID="gen34240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34241" type="x-p"/> The triumphant song being ended, and epithalamium, or marriage-song, begins, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.6">v. 6</reference>. Here observe, <div eID="gen34241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34242" type="x-p"/> I. The concert of heavenly music. The chorus was large and loud, <hi type="italic">as the voice of many waters and of mighty thunderings.</hi> God is fearful in praises. There is no discord in heaven; the morning stars sing together; no jarring string, nor key untuned, but pure and perfect melody. <div eID="gen34242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34243" type="x-p"/> II. The occasion of this song; and that is the reign and dominion of that omnipotent God who has <hi type="italic">redeemed his church by his own blood,</hi> and is now in a more public manner betrothing her to himself: <hi type="italic">The marriage of the Lamb has come,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.19.7">v. 7</reference>. Some think this refers to the conversion of the Jews, which they suppose will succeed the fall of Babylon; others, to the general resurrection: the former seems more probable. Now, 1. You have here a description of the bride, how she appeared; not in the gay and gaudy dress of the mother of harlots, but <hi type="italic">in fine linen, clean and white,</hi> which <hi type="italic">is the righteousness of saints;</hi> in the robes of Christ's righteousness, both imputed for justification and imparted for sanctification—the <hi type="italic">stola,</hi> the <hi type="italic">white robe</hi> of absolution, adoption, and enfranchisement, and the white robe of purity and universal holiness. She had <hi type="italic">washed her robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb;</hi> and these her nuptial ornaments she did not purchase by any price of her own, but received them as the gift and grant of her blessed Lord. 2. The marriage-feast, which, though not particularly described (as <reference osisRef="Matt.22.4">Matt. xxii. 4</reference>), yet is declared to be such as would make all those happy who were called to it, so called as to accept the invitation, a feast made up of the promises of the gospel, <hi type="italic">the true sayings of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.19.9">v. 9</reference>. These promises, opened, applied, sealed, and earnested by <hi type="italic">the Spirit of God,</hi> in holy eucharistical ordinances, are the marriage-feast; and the whole collective body of all those who partake of this feast is the bride, <hi type="italic">the Lamb's wife;</hi> they eat into one body, and drink into one Spirit, and are not mere spectators or guests, but coalesce into the espoused party, the mystical body of Christ. 3. The transport of joy which the apostle felt in himself at this vision. <hi type="italic">He fell down at the feet of the angel, to worship him,</hi> supposing him to be more than a creature, or having his thoughts at the present overpowered by the vehemency of his affections. Here observe, (1.) What honour he offered to the angel: <hi type="italic">He fell at his feet, to worship him;</hi> this prostration was a part of external worship, it was a posture of proper adoration. (2.) How the angel refused it, and this was with some resentment: "<hi type="italic">See thou do it not;</hi> have a care what thou doest, thou art doing a wrong thing." (3.) He gave a very good reason for his refusal: "<hi type="italic">I am thy fellow-servant, and of thy brethren which have the testimony of Jesus</hi>—I am a creature, thine equal in office, though not in nature; <hi type="italic">I,</hi> as an angel and messenger of God, <hi type="italic">have the testimony of Jesus,</hi> a charge to be a witness for him and to testify concerning him, and thou, as an apostle, having <hi type="italic">the Spirit of prophecy,</hi> hast the same testimony to give in; and therefore we are in this brethren and fellow-servants." (4.) He directs him to the true and only object of religious worship; namely, God: "<hi type="italic">Worship God,</hi> and him alone." This fully condemns both the practice of the papists in worshipping the elements of bread and wine, and saints, and angels, and the practice of those Socinians and Arians who do not believe that Christ is truly and by nature God, and yet pay him religious worship; and this shows what wretched fig-leaves all their evasions and excuses are which they offer in their own vindication: they stand hereby convicted of idolatry by a messenger from heaven.
entries.e20a59dcf56ae70a097ae1e126ecc34a15d49c17: <div eID="gen34243" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Triumph of the Saints. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 95.)</title> <div sID="gen34244" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> And I saw heaven opened, and behold a white horse; and he that sat upon him <hi type="italic">was</hi> called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he doth judge and make war. <hi type="super">12</hi> His eyes <hi type="italic">were</hi> as a flame of fire, and on his head <hi type="italic">were</hi> many crowns; and he had a name written, that no man knew, but he himself. <hi type="super">13</hi> And he <hi type="italic">was</hi> clothed with a vesture dipped in blood: and his name is called The Word of God. 14 And the armies <hi type="italic">which were</hi> in heaven followed him upon white horses, clothed in fine linen, white and clean. <hi type="super">15</hi> And out of his mouth goeth a sharp sword, that with it he should smite the nations: and he shall rule them with a rod of iron: and he treadeth the winepress of the fierceness and wrath of Almighty God. <hi type="super">16</hi> And he hath on <hi type="italic">his</hi> vesture and on his thigh a name written, <hi type="small-caps">King of kings, and Lord of lords.</hi> <hi type="super">17</hi> And I saw an angel standing in the sun; and he cried with a loud voice, saying to all the fowls that fly in the midst of heaven, Come and gather yourselves together unto the supper of the great God; <hi type="super">18</hi> That ye may eat the flesh of kings, and the flesh of captains, and the flesh of mighty men, and the flesh of horses, and of them that sit on them, and the flesh of all <hi type="italic">men, both</hi> free and bond, both small and great. <hi type="super">19</hi> And I saw the beast, and the kings of the earth, and their armies, gathered together to make war against him that sat on the horse, and against his army. <hi type="super">20</hi> And the beast was taken, and with him the false prophet that wrought miracles before him, with which he deceived them that had received the mark of the beast, and them that worshipped his image. These both were cast alive into a lake of fire burning with brimstone. <hi type="super">21</hi> And the remnant were slain with the sword of him that sat upon the horse, which <hi type="italic">sword</hi> proceeded out of his mouth: and all the fowls were filled with their flesh. <div eID="gen34244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34245" type="x-p"/> No sooner was the marriage solemnized between Christ and his church by the conversion of the Jews than the glorious head and husband of the church is called out to a new expedition, which seems to be the great battle that was to be fought at Armageddon, foretold <reference osisRef="Rev.16.16">ch. xvi. 16</reference>. And here observe, <div eID="gen34245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34246" type="x-p"/> I. The description of the great Commander, 1. By the seat of his empire; and that is <hi type="italic">heaven;</hi> his throne is there, and his power and authority are heavenly and divine. 2. His equipage: he is again described as sitting <hi type="italic">on a white horse,</hi> to show the equity of the cause, and certainty of success. 3. His attributes: he is <hi type="italic">faithful and true</hi> to his covenant and promise, he is righteous in all his judicial and military proceedings, he has a penetrating insight into all the strength and stratagems of his enemies, he has a large and extensive dominion, many crowns, for he is <hi type="italic">King of kings, and Lord of lords.</hi> 4. His armour; and that is <hi type="italic">a vesture dipped in blood,</hi> either his own blood, by which he purchased this mediatorial power, or the blood of his enemies, over whom he has always prevailed. 5. His name: <hi type="italic">The Word of God,</hi> a name that none fully knows but himself, only this we know, that this <hi type="italic">Word was God manifest in the flesh;</hi> but his perfections are incomprehensible by any creature. <div eID="gen34246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34247" type="x-p"/> II. The army which he commands (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.14">v. 14</reference>), a very large one, made up of many armies; angels and saints followed his conduct, and resembled him in their equipage, and in their armour of purity and righteousness—chosen, and called, and faithful. <div eID="gen34247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34248" type="x-p"/> III. The weapons of his warfare—<hi type="italic">A sharp sword</hi> proceeding from <hi type="italic">his mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.15">v. 15</reference>), with which <hi type="italic">he smites the nations,</hi> either the threatenings of the written word, which now he is going to execute, or rather his word of command calling on his followers to take a just revenge on his and their enemies, who are now put into the wine-press of the wrath of God, to be trodden under foot by him. <div eID="gen34248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34249" type="x-p"/> IV. The ensigns of his authority, his coat of arms—<hi type="italic">a name written on his vesture and thigh, King of kings, and Lord of lords,</hi> asserting his authority and power, and the cause of the quarrel, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.16">v. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen34249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34250" type="x-p"/> V. An invitation given <hi type="italic">to the fowls of heaven,</hi> that they should come and see the battle, and share in the spoil and pillage of the field (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.17-Rev.19.18">v. 17, 18</reference>), intimating that this great decisive engagement should leave the enemies of the church a feast for the birds of prey, and that all the world should have cause to rejoice in the issue of it. <div eID="gen34250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34251" type="x-p"/> VI. The battle joined. The enemy falls on with great fury, headed by <hi type="italic">the beast, and the kings of the earth;</hi> the powers of earth and hell gathered, to make their utmost effort, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.19">v. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen34251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34252" type="x-p"/> VII. The victory gained by the great and glorious head of the church: <hi type="italic">The beast and the false prophet,</hi> the leaders of the army, are taken prisoners, both he who led them by power and he who led them by policy and falsehood; these are taken and <hi type="italic">cast into the burning lake,</hi> made incapable of molesting the church of God any more; and their followers, whether officers or common soldiers, are given up to military execution, and made a feast for <hi type="italic">the fowls of heaven.</hi> Though the divine vengeance will chiefly fall upon <hi type="italic">the beast, and the false prophet,</hi> yet it will be no excuse to those who fight under their banner that they only followed their leaders and obeyed their command; since they would fight for them, they must fall and perish with them. <hi type="italic">Be wise now therefore, O you kings, be instructed, you rulers of the earth; kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and you perish from the way,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.10">Ps. ii. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.12">12</reference>.  <chapter eID="Rev.19"/> <div eID="gen34252" type="x-p"/>

entries.740894402087153f7fbab3f8adc275b8fa06c369: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19357"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 19</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Rev.19.1-Rev.19.21">Re 19:1-21</reference>. The Church's Thanksgiving in Heaven for the Judgment on the Harlot. The Marriage of the Lamb: The Supper: The Bride's Preparation:</title> <div sID="gen42340" type="x-p"/> John Is Forbidden to Worship the Angel: The Lord and His Hosts Come Forth for War: The Beast and the False Prophet Cast into the Lake of Fire: The Kings and Their Followers Slain by the Sword Out of Christ's Mouth.<div eID="gen42340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42341" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19357"/>1. As in the case of the opening of the prophecy, <reference osisRef="Rev.4.8">Re 4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.5.9">5:9</reference>, &c.; so now, at one of the great closing events seen in vision, the judgment on the harlot (described in <reference osisRef="Rev.18.1-Rev.18.24">Re 18:1-24</reference>), there is a song of praise in heaven to God: compare <reference osisRef="Rev.7.10">Re 7:10</reference>, &c., toward the close of the seals, and <reference osisRef="Rev.11.15-Rev.11.18">Re 11:15-18</reference>, at the close of the trumpets: <reference osisRef="Rev.15.3">Re 15:3</reference>, at the saints' victory over the beast.<div eID="gen42341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42342" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And--</hi>so Andreas. But A, B, C, Vulgate, Syriac, and Coptic omit.<div eID="gen42342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42343" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a great voice--</hi>A, B, C, Vulgate, Coptic, and Andreas read, "as it were a great voice." What a contrast to the lamentations <reference osisRef="Rev.18.1">Re 18:1</reference>-24! Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.51.48">Jr 51:48</reference>. The great manifestation of God's power in destroying Babylon calls forth a great voice of praise in heaven.<div eID="gen42343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42344" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">people--</hi>Greek, "multitude."<div eID="gen42344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42345" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Alleluia--</hi>Hebrew, "Praise ye Jah," or Jehovah: here first used in Revelation, whence Ellicott infers the Jews bear a prominent part in this thanksgiving. Jah is not a contraction of "Jehovah," as it sometimes occurs jointly with the latter. It means "He who Is": whereas Jehovah is "He who will be, is, and was." It implies God experienced as a PRESENT help; so that "Hallelujah," says Kimchi in Bengel, is found first in the Psalms on the destruction of the ungodly. "Hallelu-Jah" occurs four times in this passage. Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.149.4-Ps.149.9">Psa 149:4-9</reference>, which is plainly parallel, and indeed identical in many of the phrases, as well as the general idea. Israel, especially, will join in the Hallelujah, when "her warfare is accomplished" and her foe destroyed.<div eID="gen42345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42346" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Salvation, &c.--</hi>Greek, "The salvation ... the glory ... the power."<div eID="gen42346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42347" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and honour--</hi>so Coptic. But A, B, C, and Syriac omit.<div eID="gen42347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42348" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the Lord our God--</hi>so Andreas. But A, B, C, and Coptic read, "(Is) of our God," that is, belongs to Him. <div eID="gen42348" type="x-p"/>
entries.7c54dc77b013ba17a113875a904e8d6eeb4525ed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19358"/><div sID="gen42349" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19358"/><hi type="bold">2. which did corrupt the earth--</hi>Greek, "used to corrupt" continually. "Instead of opposing and lessening, she promoted the sinful life and decay of the world by her own earthliness, allowing the salt to lose its savor" [Auberlen].<div eID="gen42349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42350" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">avenged--</hi>Greek, "exacted in retribution." A particular application of the principle (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.5">Ge 9:5</reference>).<div eID="gen42350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42351" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blood of his servants--</hi>literally shed by the Old Testament adulterous Church, and by the New Testament apostate Church; also virtually, though not literally, by all who, though called Christians, hate their brother, or love not the brethren of Christ, but shrink from the reproach of the cross, and show unkindness towards those who bear it. <div eID="gen42351" type="x-p"/>
entries.9be084ca32ef1b83afcce822afd5f0a16c8a3569: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19359"/><div sID="gen42352" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19359"/><hi type="bold">3. again--</hi>Greek, "a second time."<div eID="gen42352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42353" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rose up--</hi>Greek, "goeth up."<div eID="gen42353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42354" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for ever and ever--</hi>Greek, "to the ages of the ages." <div eID="gen42354" type="x-p"/>
entries.1034cdb3d2f97873ac5285f1e39f4c46f4f0bfe2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19360"/><div sID="gen42355" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19360"/><hi type="bold">4. beasts--</hi>rather, "living creatures."<div eID="gen42355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42356" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sat--</hi>Greek, "sitteth." <div eID="gen42356" type="x-p"/>
entries.935db7814965ec9167448e4867a7526a9f0ccb16: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19361"/><div sID="gen42357" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19361"/><hi type="bold">5. out of--</hi>Greek, "out from the throne" in A, B, C.<div eID="gen42357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42358" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Praise our God--</hi>Compare the solemn act of praise performed by the Levites, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.36">1Ch 16:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.23.5">23:5</reference>, especially when the house of God was filled with the divine glory (<reference osisRef="2Chr.5.13">2Ch 5:13</reference>).<div eID="gen42358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42359" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">both--</hi>omitted in A, B, C, Vulgate, Coptic, and Syriac. Translate as Greek, "the small and the great." <div eID="gen42359" type="x-p"/>
entries.ab745c88aeb770c6bb878867f5b58510d6cc4d58: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19362"/><div sID="gen42360" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19362"/><hi type="bold">6. many waters--</hi>Contrast the "many waters" on which the whore sitteth (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.1">Re 17:1</reference>). This verse is the hearty response to the stirring call, "Alleluia! Praise our God" (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.4">Re 19:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.5">5</reference>).<div eID="gen42360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42361" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord God omnipotent--</hi>Greek, "the Omnipotent."<div eID="gen42361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42362" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reigneth--</hi>literally, "reigned": hence reigneth once for all. His reign is a fact already established. Babylon, the harlot, was one great hindrance to His reign being recognized. Her overthrow now clears the way for His advent to reign; therefore, not merely Rome, but the whole of Christendom in so far as it is carnal and compromised Christ for the world, is comprehended in the term "harlot." The beast hardly arises when he at once "goeth into perdition": so that Christ is prophetically considered as already reigning, so soon does His advent follow the judgment on the harlot. <div eID="gen42362" type="x-p"/>
entries.cc56b696d4400ad3a17b2bd90a08e86a8550b068: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19363"/><div sID="gen42363" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19363"/><hi type="bold">7. glad ... rejoice--</hi>Greek, "rejoice ... exult."<div eID="gen42363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42364" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">give--</hi>so B and Andreas. But A reads, "we will give."<div eID="gen42364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42365" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">glory--</hi>Greek, "the glory."<div eID="gen42365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42366" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the marriage of the Lamb is come--</hi>The full and final consummation is at <reference osisRef="Rev.21.2-Rev.21.9">Re 21:2-9</reference>, &c. Previously there must be the overthrow of the beast, &c., at the Lord's coming, the binding of Satan, the millennial reign, the loosing of Satan and his last overthrow, and the general judgment. The elect-Church, the heavenly Bride, soon after the destruction of the harlot, is transfigured at the Lord's coming, and joins with Him in His triumph over the beast. On the emblem of the heavenly Bridegroom and Bride, compare <reference osisRef="Matt.22.2">Mt 22:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.6">25:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.2">2Co 11:2</reference>. Perfect union with Him personally, and participation in His holiness; joy, glory, and kingdom, are included in this symbol of "marriage"; compare Song of Solomon everywhere. Besides the heavenly Bride, the transfigured, translated, and risen Church, reigning over the earth with Christ, there is also the earthly bride, Israel, in the flesh, never yet divorced, though for a time separated, from her divine husband, who shall then be reunited to the Lord, and be the mother Church of the millennial earth, Christianized through her. Note, we ought, as Scripture does, restrict the language drawn from marriage-love to the Bride, the Church as a whole; not use it as individuals in our relation to Christ, which Rome does in the case of her nuns. Individually, believers are effectually-called guests; collectively, they constitute the bride. The harlot divides her affections among many lovers: the bride gives hers exclusively to Christ. <div eID="gen42366" type="x-p"/>
entries.928d6f9edcb448da3c476ebad1278ad137b61ab5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19364"/><div sID="gen42367" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19364"/><hi type="bold">8. granted--</hi>Though in one sense she "made herself ready," having by the Spirit's work in her put on "the wedding garment," yet in the fullest sense it is not she, but her Lord, who makes her ready by "granting to her that she be arrayed in fine linen." It is He who, by giving Himself for her, presents her to Himself a glorious Church, not having spot, but holy and without blemish. It is He also who sanctifies her, naturally vile and without beauty, with the washing of water by the word, and puts His own comeliness on her, which thus becomes hers.<div eID="gen42367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42368" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">clean and white--</hi>so Andreas. But A and B transpose. Translate, "bright and pure"; at once brilliantly splendid and spotless as in the bride herself.<div eID="gen42368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42369" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteousness--</hi>Greek, "righteousnesses"; distributively used. Each saint must have this righteousness: not merely be justified, as if the righteousness belonged to the Church in the aggregate; the saints together have righteousnesses; namely, He is accounted as "the Lord our righteousness" to each saint on his believing, their robes being made white in the blood of the Lamb. The righteousness of the saint is not, as Alford erroneously states, inherent, but is imputed: if it were otherwise, Christ would be merely enabling the sinner to justify himself. <reference osisRef="Rom.5.18">Ro 5:18</reference> is decisive on this. Compare Article XI, Church of England. The justification already given to the saints in title and unseen possession, is now GIVEN them in manifestation: they openly walk with Christ in white. To this, rather than to their primary justification on earth, the reference is here. Their justification before the apostate world, which had persecuted them, contrasts with the judgment and condemnation of the harlot. "Now that the harlot has fallen, the woman triumphs" [Auberlen]. Contrast with the pure fine linen (indicating the simplicity and purity) of the bride, the tawdry ornamentation of the harlot. Babylon, the apostate Church, is the antithesis to new Jerusalem, the transfigured Church of God. The woman (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.1-Rev.12.6">Re 12:1-6</reference>), the harlot (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.1-Rev.17.7">Re 17:1-7</reference>), the bride (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.1-Rev.19.10">Re 19:1-10</reference>), are the three leading aspects of the Church. <div eID="gen42369" type="x-p"/>
entries.2ee5b41dfa7a8de8fcc6e360378a9d729be0d826: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19365"/><div sID="gen42370" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19365"/><hi type="bold">9. He--</hi>God by His angel saith unto me.<div eID="gen42370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42371" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">called--</hi>effectually, not merely externally. The "unto," or into," seems to express this: not merely invited to (Greek, "epi"), but called INTO, so as to be partakers of (Greek, "eis"); compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">1Co 1:9</reference>.<div eID="gen42371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42372" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">marriage supper--</hi>Greek, "the supper of the marriage." Typified by the Lord's Supper.<div eID="gen42372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42373" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">true--</hi>Greek, "genuine"; veritable sayings which shall surely be fulfilled, namely, all the previous revelations. <div eID="gen42373" type="x-p"/>
entries.98fbb189caa942bac29e63cb6c0dc09470978180: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19366"/><div sID="gen42374" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19366"/><hi type="bold">10. at--</hi>Greek, "before." John's intending to worship the angel here, as in <reference osisRef="Rev.22.8">Re 22:8</reference>, on having revealed to him the glory of the new Jerusalem, is the involuntary impulse of adoring joy at so blessed a prospect. It forms a marked contrast to the sorrowful wonder with which he had looked on the Church in her apostasy as the harlot (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.6">Re 17:6</reference>). It exemplifies the corrupt tendencies of our fallen nature that even John, an apostle, should have all but fallen into "voluntary humility and worshipping of angels," which Paul warns us against.<div eID="gen42374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42375" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and of thy brethren--</hi>that is, a fellow servant of thy brethren.<div eID="gen42375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42376" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have the testimony of Jesus--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Rev.12.17">Re 12:17</reference>).<div eID="gen42376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42377" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the testimony of--</hi>that is, respecting Jesus.<div eID="gen42377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42378" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is the spirit of prophecy--</hi>is the result of the same spirit of prophecy in you as in myself. We angels, and you apostles, all alike have the testimony of (bear testimony concerning) Jesus by the operation of one and the same Spirit, who enables me to show you these revelations and enables you to record them: wherefore we are fellow servants, not I your lord to be worshipped by you. Compare <reference osisRef="Rev.22.9">Re 22:9</reference>, "I am fellow servant of thee and of thy brethren the prophets"; whence the "FOR the testimony," &c., here, may be explained as giving the reason for his adding "and (fellow servant) of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus." I mean, of the prophets; "for it is of Jesus that thy brethren, the prophets, testify by the Spirit in them." A clear condemnation of Romish invocation of saints as if they were our superiors to be adored. <div eID="gen42378" type="x-p"/>
entries.96a84cecd837589a2cd5244a002aaa4ae43337f8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19367"/><div sID="gen42379" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19367"/><hi type="bold">11. behold a white horse; and he that sat upon him--</hi>identical with <reference osisRef="Rev.6.2">Re 6:2</reference>. Here as there he comes forth "conquering and to conquer." Compare the ass-colt on which He rode into Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.1-Matt.21.7">Mt 21:1-7</reference>). The horse was used for war: and here He is going forth to war with the beast. The ass is for peace. His riding on it into Jerusalem is an earnest of His reign in Jerusalem over the earth, as the Prince of peace, after all hostile powers have been overthrown. When the security of the world power, and the distress of the people of God, have reached the highest point, the Lord Jesus shall appear visibly from heaven to put an end to the whole course of the world, and establish His kingdom of glory. He comes to judge with vengeance the world power, and to bring to the Church redemption, transfiguration, and power over the world. Distinguish between this coming (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.27">Mt 24:27</reference>, 29, 37, 39; Greek, "parousia") and the end, or final judgment (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.31">Mt 25:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.23">1Co 15:23</reference>). Powerful natural phenomena shall accompany His advent [Auberlen]. <div eID="gen42379" type="x-p"/>
entries.5ad7b055025764aeab0e4649183513d86426eae7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19368"/><div sID="gen42380" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19368"/>12. Identifying Him with the Son of man similarly described, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.14">Re 1:14</reference>.<div eID="gen42380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42381" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">many crowns--</hi>Greek, "diadems": not merely (Greek, "stephanoi") garlands of victory, but royal crowns, as King of kings. Christ's diadem comprises all the diadems of the earth and of heavenly powers too. Contrast the papal tiara composed of three diadems. Compare also the little horn (Antichrist) that overcomes the three horns or kingdoms, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.8">Da 7:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.24">24</reference> (Quære, the Papacy? or some three kingdoms that succeed the papacy, which itself, as a temporal kingdom, was made up at first of three kingdoms, the exarchate of Ravenna, the kingdom of the Lombards, and the state of Rome, obtained by Pope Zachary and Stephen II from Pepin, the usurper of the French dominion). Also, the seven crowns (diadems) on the seven heads of the dragon (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.3">Re 12:3</reference>), and ten diadems on the ten heads of the beast. These usurpers claim the diadems which belong to Christ alone.<div eID="gen42381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42382" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he had a name written--</hi>B and Syriac insert, "He had names written, and a name written," &c., meaning that the names of the dominion which each diadem indicated were written on them severally. But A, Vulgate, Origen, and Cyprian omits the words, as English Version.<div eID="gen42382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42383" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">name ... that no man knew but ... himself--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Judg.13.18">Jud 13:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.9">1Co 2:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.3.2">1Jo 3:2</reference>). The same is said of the "new name" of believers. In this, as in all other respects, the disciple is made like his Lord. The Lord's own "new name" is to be theirs, and to be "in their foreheads"; whence we may infer that His as yet unknown name also is written on His forehead; as the high priest had "Holiness to the Lord" inscribed on the miter on his brow. John saw it as "written," but knew not its meaning. It is, therefore, a name which in all its glorious significancy can be only understood when the union of His saints with Him, and His and their joint triumph and reign, shall be perfectly manifested at the final consummation. <div eID="gen42383" type="x-p"/>
entries.c139fbedc0ae801b0d0b6a19cef054aa9fd913bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19369"/><div sID="gen42384" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19369"/><hi type="bold">13. vesture dipped in blood--</hi><reference osisRef="Isa.63.2">Is 63:2</reference> is alluded to here, and in <reference osisRef="Rev.19.15">Re 19:15</reference>, end. There the blood is not His own, but that of His foes. So here the blood on His "vesture," reminding us of His own blood shed for even the ungodly who trample on it, is a premonition of the shedding of their blood in righteous retribution. He sheds the blood, not of the godly, as the harlot and beast did, but of the blood-stained ungodly, including them both.<div eID="gen42384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42385" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The Word of God--</hi>who made the world, is He also who under the same character and attributes shall make it anew. His title, Son of God, is applicable in a lower sense, also to His people; but "the Word of God" indicates His incommunicable Godhead, joined to His manhood, which He shall then manifest in glory. "The Bride does not fear the Bridegroom; her love casteth out fear. She welcomes Him; she cannot be happy but at His side. The Lamb [Re 19:9, the aspect of Christ to His people at His coming] is the symbol of Christ in His gentleness. Who would be afraid of a lamb? Even a little child, instead of being scared, desires to caress it. There is nothing to make us afraid of God but sin, and Jesus is the Lamb of God that taketh away the sin of the world. What a fearful contrast is the aspect which He will wear towards His enemies! Not as the Bridegroom and the Lamb, but as the [avenging] judge and warrior stained in the blood of His enemies." <div eID="gen42385" type="x-p"/>
entries.5010d91accbbe93d60467564dfecf0a5b937fa34: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19370"/><div sID="gen42386" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19370"/><hi type="bold">14. the armies ... in heaven--</hi>Compare "the horse bridles," <reference osisRef="Rev.14.20">Re 14:20</reference>. The glorified saints whom God "will bring with" Christ at His advent; compare <reference osisRef="Rev.17.14">Re 17:14</reference>, "they that are with Him, called, chosen, faithful"; as also "His mighty angels."<div eID="gen42386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42387" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">white and clean--</hi>Greek, "pure." A, B, Vulgate, Syriac, and Cyprian omit "and," which Origen and Andreas retain, as English Version. <div eID="gen42387" type="x-p"/>
entries.25535ce7cad4a9635d661dcccbedd2b481566020: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19371"/><div sID="gen42388" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19371"/><hi type="bold">15. out of his mouth ... sword--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rev.1.16">Re 1:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.16">2:12, 16</reference>). Here in its avenging power, <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.8">2Th 2:8</reference>, "consume with the Spirit of His mouth" (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Is 11:4</reference>, to which there is allusion here); not in its convicting and converting efficacy (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.17">Ep 6:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.4.12">He 4:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.4.13">13</reference>, where also the judicial keenness of the sword-like word is included). The Father commits the judgment to the Son.<div eID="gen42388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42389" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he shall rule--</hi>The HE is emphatic, He and none other, in contrast to the usurpers who have misruled on earth. "Rule," literally, "tend as a shepherd"; but here in a punitive sense. He, who would have shepherded them with pastoral rod and with the golden scepter of His love, shall dash them in pieces, as refractory rebels, with "a rod of iron."<div eID="gen42389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42390" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">treadeth ... wine-press--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.63.3">Is 63:3</reference>).<div eID="gen42390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42391" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the fierceness and wrath--</hi>So Andreas reads. But A, B, Vulgate, Coptic, and Origen read, "of the fierceness (or boiling indignation) of the wrath," omitting "and."<div eID="gen42391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42392" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Almighty--</hi>The fierceness of Christ's wrath against His foes will be executed with the resources of omnipotence. <div eID="gen42392" type="x-p"/>
entries.7cd91d426d3504156670485f0cf29d1411aa671e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19372"/><div sID="gen42393" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19372"/>16. "His name written on His vesture and on His thigh," was written partly on the vesture, partly on the thigh itself, at the part where in an equestrian figure the robe drops from the thigh. The thigh symbolizes Christ's humanity as having come, after the flesh, from the loins of David, and now appearing as the glorified "Son of man." On the other hand, His incommunicable divine name, "which no man knew," is on His head (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.12">Re 19:12</reference>), [Menochius].<div eID="gen42393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42394" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">KING OF KINGS--</hi>Compare <reference osisRef="Rev.17.14">Re 17:14</reference>, in contrast with <reference osisRef="Rev.19.17">Re 19:17</reference>, the beast being in attempted usurpation a king of kings, the ten kings delivering their kingdom to him. <div eID="gen42394" type="x-p"/>
entries.955385e29f9edbe10ae56d6dc0131f688da90f50: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19373"/><div sID="gen42395" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19373"/><hi type="bold">17. an--</hi>Greek, "one."<div eID="gen42395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42396" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the sun--</hi>so as to be conspicuous in sight of the whole world.<div eID="gen42396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42397" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to all the fowls--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.39.17-Ezek.39.20">Eze 39:17-20</reference>).<div eID="gen42397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42398" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and gather yourselves--</hi>A, B, Vulgate, Syriac, Coptic, and Andreas read, "be gathered," omitting "and."<div eID="gen42398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42399" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the great God--</hi>A, B, Vulgate, Syriac, Coptic, and Andreas read, "the great supper (that is, banquet) of God." <div eID="gen42399" type="x-p"/>
entries.c3bab4ffe04e6bf04659b81cf3804a22faf06968: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19374"/><div sID="gen42400" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19374"/>18. Contrast with this "supper," <reference osisRef="Rev.19.17">Re 19:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.18">18</reference>, the marriage supper of the Lamb, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.9">Re 19:9</reference>.<div eID="gen42400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42401" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">captains--</hi>Greek, "captains of thousands," that is, chief captains. The "kings" are "the ten" who "give their power unto the beast."<div eID="gen42401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42402" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">free and bond--</hi>specified in <reference osisRef="Rev.13.16">Re 13:16</reference>, as "receiving the mark of the beast." The repetition of flesh (in the Greek it is plural: masses of flesh) five times in this verse, marks the gross carnality of the followers of the beast. Again, the giving of their flesh to the fowls to eat, is a righteous retribution for their not suffering the dead bodies of Christ's witnesses to be put in graves. <div eID="gen42402" type="x-p"/>
entries.84a70949aae9f8e64b4a07bb69adf150ce1ece60: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19375"/><div sID="gen42403" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19375"/><hi type="bold">19. gathered together--</hi>at Armageddon, under the sixth vial. For "their armies" in B and Andreas, there is found "His armies" in A.<div eID="gen42403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42404" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">war--</hi>so Andreas. But A and B read, "the war," namely, that foretold, <reference osisRef="Rev.16.14">Re 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.17.4">17:4</reference>. <div eID="gen42404" type="x-p"/>
entries.a7b96429f5a092f6dc716354b3db63ed290de784: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19376"/><div sID="gen42405" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19376"/><hi type="bold">20. and with him the false prophet--</hi>A reads, "and those with him." B reads, "and he who was with him, the false prophet."<div eID="gen42405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42406" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">miracles--</hi>Greek, "the miracles" (literally, "signs") recorded already (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.14">Re 13:14</reference>) as wrought by the second beast before (literally, 'in sight of') the first beast. Hence it follows the second beast is identical with the false prophet. Many expositors represent the first beast to be the secular, the second beast to be the ecclesiastical power of Rome; and account for the change of title for the latter from the "other beast" to the "false prophet," is because by the judgment on the harlot, the ecclesiastical power will then retain nothing of its former character save the power to deceive. I think it not unlikely that the false prophet will be the successor of the spiritual pretensions of the papacy; while the beast in its last form as the fully revealed Antichrist will be the secular representative and embodiment of the fourth world kingdom, Rome, in its last form of intensified opposition to God. Compare with this prophecy, <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.1-Ezek.39.29">Eze 38:1-39:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.2.34">Da 2:34</reference>, 35, 44; 11:44, 45; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.1">12:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.3.9-Joel.3.17">Joe 3:9-17</reference>; Zec 12:<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.21">1-14:21</reference>. Daniel (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.8">Da 7:8</reference>) makes no mention of the second beast, or false prophet, but mentions that "the little horn" has "the eyes of a man," that is, cunning and intellectual culture; this is not a feature of the first beast in the thirteenth chapter, but is expressed by the Apocalyptic "false prophet," the embodiment of man's unsanctified knowledge, and the subtlety of the old serpent. The first beast is a political power; the second is a spiritual power--the power of ideas. But both are beasts, the worldly Antichristian wisdom serving the worldly Antichristian power. The dragon is both lion and serpent. As the first law in God's moral government is that "judgment should begin at the house of God," and be executed on the harlot, the faithless Church, by the world power with which she had committed spiritual adultery, so it is a second law that the world power, after having served as God's instrument of punishment, is itself punished. As the harlot is judged by the beast and the ten kings, so these are destroyed by the Lord Himself coming in person. So <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.1-Zeph.1.18">Zep 1:1-18</reference> compared with <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.1-Zeph.2.15">Zep 2:1-15</reference>. And Jeremiah, after denouncing Jerusalem's judgment by Babylon, ends with denouncing Babylon's own doom. Between the judgment on the harlot and the Lord's destruction of the beast, will intervene that season in which earthly-mindedness will reach its culmination, and Antichristianity triumph for its short three and a half days during which the two witnesses lie dead. Then shall the Church be ripe for her glorification, the Antichristian world for destruction. The world at the highest development of its material and spiritual power is but a decorated carcass round which the eagles gather. It is characteristic that Antichrist and his kings, in their blindness, imagine that they can wage war against the King of heaven with earthly hosts; herein is shown the extreme folly of Babylonian confusion. The Lord's mere appearance, without any actual encounter, shows Antichrist his nothingness; compare the effect of Jesus' appearance even in His humiliation, <reference osisRef="John.18.6">Joh 18:6</reference> [Auberlen].<div eID="gen42406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42407" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">had received--</hi>rather as Greek, "received," once for all.<div eID="gen42407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42408" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them; that worshipped--</hi>literally, "them worshipping" not an act once for all done, as the "received" implies, but those in the habit of "worshipping."<div eID="gen42408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42409" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">These both were cast ... into a lake--</hi>Greek, "... the lake of fire," Gehenna. Satan is subsequently cast into it, at the close of the outbreak which succeeds the millennium (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.10">Re 20:10</reference>). Then Death and Hell, as well those not found at the general judgment "written in the book of life"; this constitutes "the second death."<div eID="gen42409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42410" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">alive--</hi>a living death; not mere annihilation. "Their worm dieth not, their fire is not quenched." <div eID="gen42410" type="x-p"/>
entries.e43dd6d3fa8eb00cbb4b5b2091af1e15438e2797: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19377"/><div sID="gen42411" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19377"/><hi type="bold">21. the remnant--</hi>Greek, "the rest," that is, "the kings and their armies" (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.19">Re 19:19</reference>) classed together in one indiscriminate mass. A solemn confirmation of the warning in <reference osisRef="Ps.2.10">Psa 2:10</reference>. <chapter eID="Rev.19"/>

entries.70c149b52c31a7a578c201c31f477170e95ddb8c: <div eID="gen56639" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen56640" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen56641" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen56641" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen56640" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen56642" type="x-p"/> The whole heavenly host give glory to God, because he has judged the great whore, and avenged the blood of his saints, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.1-Rev.19.6">Rev 19:1-6</reference>. The marriage of the Lamb and his bride, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.7-Rev.19.9">Rev 19:7-9</reference>. John offers to worship the angel, but is prevented, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.10">Rev 19:10</reference>. Heaven is opened, and Jesus the Word of God appears on a white horse; he and his armies described, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.11-Rev.19.16">Rev 19:11-16</reference>. An angel in the sun invites all the fowls of heaven to come to the supper of the great God, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.17">Rev 19:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.18">Rev 19:18</reference>. The beast, the false prophet, and the kings of the earth, gather together to make war with him who sits on the white horse; but they are all discomfited, and utterly destroyed, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.19-Rev.19.21">Rev 19:19-21</reference>. <div eID="gen56642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56643" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen56643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56644" type="x-p"/> I heard a great voice of much people in heaven - The idolatrous city being destroyed, and the blood of the martyred saints being avenged, there is a universal joy among the redeemed of the Lord, which they commence with the word הללו יה Hallelu-Yah, praise ye Jah or Jehovah; which the Septuagint, and St. John from them, put into Greek letters thus: Αλληλουΐα, Allelou-ia, a form of praise which the heathens appear to have borrowed from the Jews, as is evident from their paeans, or hymns in honor of Apollo, which began and ended with ελελευ ιη, eleleu ie; a mere corruption of the Hebrew words. It is worthy of remark that the Indians of North America have the same word in their religious worship, and use it in the same sense. "In their places of worship, or beloved square, they dance sometimes for a whole night always in a bowing posture, and frequently singing halleluyah Ye ho wah; praise ye Yah, Ye ho vah:" probably the true pronunciation of the Hebrew יהוה, which we call Jehovah. See Adair's History of the American Indians. <div eID="gen56644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56645" type="x-p"/> Salvation - He is the sole author of deliverance from sin; the glory of this belongs to him, the honor should be ascribed to him, and his power is that alone by which it is effected.
entries.54fb88367ec62b551b5c0041241d31d83373aaaf: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen56645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56646" type="x-p"/> For true and righteous - His judgments displayed in supporting his followers, and punishing his enemies, are true - according to his predictions; and righteous, being all according to infinite justice and equity.
entries.39f2062ff61b4e46481b9ceee24c89b49efe942a: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen56646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56647" type="x-p"/> Her smoke rose up - There was, and shall be, a continual evidence of God's judgments executed on this great whore or idolatrous city; nor shall it ever be restored.
entries.478b95baf8338bb267b0533a518b3ed073dc2033: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen56647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56648" type="x-p"/> The four and twenty elders - The true Church of the Lord Jesus converted from among the Jews. See <reference osisRef="Rev.4.10">Rev 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.5.14">Rev 5:14</reference>.
entries.265a38c753e71ea5569eb2a1a4a65bbaf2414c32: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen56648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56649" type="x-p"/> Praise our God, etc. - Let all, whether redeemed from among Jews or Gentiles, give glory to God.
entries.97093a30de42716a214ed01f2add9e8398cce190: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen56649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56650" type="x-p"/> The voice of a great multitude - This is the catholic or universal Church of God gathered from among the Gentiles. <div eID="gen56650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56651" type="x-p"/> The Lord God Omnipotent reigneth - Εβασιλευσε Κυριος ὁ Θεος ὁ παντοκρατωρ. Many excellent MSS., most of the versions, with Andreas and Arethas, the two most ancient commentators on this book, add ἡμων, our, after ὁ Θεος· and according to this the text reads emphatically thus: Our Lord God, the Almighty, reigneth. What consolation to every genuine Christian that His Lord and God is the Almighty, and that this Almighty never trusts the reins of the government of the universe out of his hands! What therefore has his Church to fear?
entries.8de56593c9d953984adba2b51146adaa68151fe0: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen56651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56652" type="x-p"/> The marriage of the Lamb is come - The meaning of these figurative expressions appears to be this: After this overthrow of idolatry and superstition, and the discomfiture of antichrist, there will be a more glorious state of Christianity than ever was before.
entries.2b6fd70a69f1b0b5a1bfb30f36f34894804a1330: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen56652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56653" type="x-p"/> Arrayed in fine linen - A prediction that the Church should become more pure in her doctrines, more pious in her experience, and more righteous in her conduct, than she had ever been from her formation. <div eID="gen56653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56654" type="x-p"/> The fine linen here spoken of is not the righteousness of Christ imputed to believers, for it is here called the righteousness of the saints - that which the grace and Spirit of Christ has wrought in them.
entries.3e26fdfd7287675e5d347182954acca9dc05bf5a: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen56654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56655" type="x-p"/> Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper - This is an evident allusion to the marriage of the king's son, <reference osisRef="Mat.22.2">Mat 22:2</reference>, etc., where the incarnation of our Lord, and the calling of Jews and Gentiles, are particularly pointed out. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Mat.22.2">Mat 22:2</reference>. Blessed are all they who hear the Gospel, and are thus invited to lay hold on everlasting life.
entries.e8ab4a0782517519768cc2ac3ce6022bc5bb7243: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen56655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56656" type="x-p"/> I fell at his feet to worship him - Great as this angel was, St. John could not mistake him either for Jesus Christ, or for God the Father; nor was his prostration intended as an act of religious worship. It was merely an act of that sort of reverence which any Asiatic would pay to a superior. His mistake was, the considering that he was under obligation to the angel for the information which he had now received. This mistake the angel very properly corrects, showing him that it was from God alone this intelligence came, and that to him alone the praise was due. <div eID="gen56656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56657" type="x-p"/> I am thy fellow servant - No higher in dignity than thyself; employed by the same God, on the same errand, and with the same testimony; and therefore not entitled to thy prostration: worship God - prostrate thyself to him, and to him give thanks. <div eID="gen56657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56658" type="x-p"/> The testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy - As this is a reason given by the angel why he should not worship him, the meaning must be this: I, who have received this spirit of prophecy, am not superior to thee who hast received the testimony of Christ, to preach him among the Gentiles; for the commission containing such a testimony is equal to the gift of the spirit of prophecy. Or, the spirit of prophecy is a general testimony concerning Jesus, for he is the scope and design of the whole Scripture; to him gave all the prophets witness. Take Jesus, his grace, Spirit, and religion out of the Bible, and it has neither scope, design, object, nor end.
entries.3ce36252677fca36bada948f8afcaabd9de9f9eb: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen56658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56659" type="x-p"/> A white horse - This is an exhibition of the triumph of Christ after the destruction of his enemies. The white horse is the emblem of this, and Faithful and True are characters of Christ. See <reference osisRef="Rev.3.14">Rev 3:14</reference>. <div eID="gen56659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56660" type="x-p"/> In righteousness he doth judge and make war - The wars which he wages are from no principle of ambition, lust of power, or extension of conquest and dominion; they are righteous in their principle and in their object. And this is perhaps what no earthly potentate could ever say.
entries.9bb9446313f5e12fc065a86be2314fdc12bfcc4c: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen56660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56661" type="x-p"/> His eyes were as a flame of fire - To denote the piercing and all-penetrating nature of his wisdom. <div eID="gen56661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56662" type="x-p"/> On his head were many crowns - To denote the multitude of his conquests, and the extent of his dominion. <div eID="gen56662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56663" type="x-p"/> A name written, that no man knew - This is a reference to what the rabbins call the shem hammephorash, or tetragrammaton, יהוה Yhvh; or what we call Jehovah. This name the Jews never attempt to pronounce: when they meet with it in the Bible, they read אדני Adonai for it; but, to a man, they all declare that no man can pronounce it; and that the true pronunciation has been lost, at least since the Babylonish captivity; and that God alone knows its true interpretation and pronunciation. This, therefore, is the name which no man knew but he himself.
entries.e7e2472b6b19e92eae0140a78fba31af6cf87c09: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen56663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56664" type="x-p"/> He was clothed with a vesture dipped in blood - To show that he was just come from recent slaughter. The description is taken from <reference osisRef="Isa.63.2">Isa 63:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.3">Isa 63:3</reference>, where Judas Maccabeus, or some other conqueror, is described. <div eID="gen56664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56665" type="x-p"/> The Word of God - Written in the Targum, and in other Jewish writings, מימרא דיי meimera daiya, "the word of Jehovah;" by which they always mean a person, and not a word spoken. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Joh.1.1">Joh 1:1</reference>, etc.
entries.22d5beed7dcfc91dbb42d2d5f322dbae14488e3b: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen56665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56666" type="x-p"/> The armies which were in heaven - Angels and saints over whom Jesus Christ is Captain, <div eID="gen56666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56667" type="x-p"/> Clothed in fine linen - All holy, pure, and righteous.
entries.77913c18e93f1f9b09069722e08d5f905422bcb9: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen56667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56668" type="x-p"/> Out of his mouth goeth a sharp sword - See on <reference osisRef="Rev.1.16">Rev 1:16</reference> (note). This appears to mean the word of the Gospel, by which his enemies are confounded, and his friends supported and comforted. <div eID="gen56668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56669" type="x-p"/> With a rod of iron - He shall execute the severest judgment on the opposers of his truth. <div eID="gen56669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56670" type="x-p"/> He treaded the winepress - As the grapes are trodden to express the juice, so his enemies shall be bruised and beaten, so that their life's blood shall be poured out.
entries.031557cf3b349ca077d6025b51d6170cd55b2e2c: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen56670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56671" type="x-p"/> On his vesture and on his thigh a name written - Dr. Dodd has well observed on this passage, that "it appears to have been an ancient custom among several nations to adorn the images of their deities, princes, victors at public games, and other eminent persons, with inscriptions, expressing either the character of the persons, their names, or some other circumstance which might contribute to their honor; and to that custom the description here given of Christ may possibly have some allusion. "There are several such images yet extant, with an inscription written either on the garment, or on one of the thighs, or on that part of the garment which was over the thigh; and probably this is the meaning of the apostle. And as these inscriptions are placed on the upper garment, Grotius seems very justly to have explained the words επι το ἱματιον, by his imperial robe, that his power in this victory might be conspicuous to all. But as a farther confirmation of this sense of the passage it may not be improper here to describe briefly several remarkable figures of this sort, which are still extant." This description I shall give from my own examination. <div eID="gen56671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56672" type="x-p"/> 1. Herodotus, Euterpe, lib. ii. p. 127, edit. Gale, speaking of the actions of Sesostris, and of the images he set up in the countries which he conquered, has the following words: Εισι δε περι Ιωνιην δυο τυποι εν πετρῃσι εγκεκολαμμενοι τουτου του ανδρος, κ. τ. λ. "Two images likewise of this man are seen in Ionia, on the way that leads from Ephesus to Phocaea, and from Sardis to Smyrna. The figure is five palms in height; in his right hand he holds a dart, in his left a bow, armed after the manner of the Egyptians and Ethiopians. On a line drawn across the breast, from one shoulder to the other, are these words, written in Egyptian hieroglyphics: Εγω τηνδε την χωρην ωμοισι τοισι εμοισι εκτησαμην· 'I obtained this country by these my shoulders;'" i.e., by my own power. <div eID="gen56672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56673" type="x-p"/> 2. In the Etruria Regalis of Dempster, in the appendix at the end of vol. ii., there is a beautiful female figure of brass, about twelve inches high, the hair gracefully plaited, and the head adorned with a diadem. She has a tunic without sleeves, and over that a sort of pallium. On the outside of the right thigh, close to the tunic, and probably on it, in the original, is an inscription in Etruscan characters. What these import I cannot say. Dempster has given a general explanation of the image in the appendix to the above volume, p. 108. The plate itself is the eighty-third of the work. <div eID="gen56673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56674" type="x-p"/> 3. There are two other images found in the same author, vol. i., p. 91, tab. xxiv.; the first is naked, with the exception of a short loose jupe, or petticoat, which goes round the loins, and over the left arm. On the left thigh of this image there is an inscription in Etruscan characters. The second has a similar jupe, but much longer, which extends to the calf of the leg, and is supported over the bended left arm. Over the right thigh, on this vesture, there is an Etruscan inscription in two lines. <div eID="gen56674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56675" type="x-p"/> 4. Montfaucon, Antiquite Expliquee, vol. iii., part 2, p. 268, has introduced an account of two fine images, which are represented tab. CLVII. The first is a warrior entirely naked, except a collar, one bracelet, and boots. On his left thigh, extending from the groin to a little below the knee, is an inscription in very ancient Etruscan characters, in two lines, but the import is unknown. <div eID="gen56675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56676" type="x-p"/> The second is a small figure of brass, about six inches long, with a loose tunic, which is suspended from the left shoulder down to the calf of the legs. On this tunic, over the left thigh, is an inscription (perhaps) in very ancient Latin characters, but in the Etruscan language, as the learned author conjectures. It is in one line, but what it means is equally unknown. <div eID="gen56676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56677" type="x-p"/> 5. In the same work, p. 269, tab. CLVIII., another Etruscan warrior is represented entirely naked; on the left thigh is the following words in uncial Greek letters, ΚΑΦΙΣΟΔΩΡΟΣ, and on the right thigh, ΑΙΣΧΛΑΜΙΟΥ, i.e., "Kaphisodorus, the son of Aischlamius." All these inscriptions are written longitudinally on the thigh. <div eID="gen56677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56678" type="x-p"/> 6. Gruter, vol. iii., p. DCCCCLXXXIX, sub. tit. Affectus Servorum et Libertinorum inter se, et in suos, gives us the figure of a naked warrior, with his left hand on an axe, the end of whose helve rests on the ground, with the following inscription on the inside of his left thigh, longitudinally written, as in all other cases: - <div eID="gen56678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56679" type="x-p"/> A. Poblicius. D. L. Antioc. <div eID="gen56679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56680" type="x-p"/> Ti. Barbius. Q. P. L. Tiber. <div eID="gen56680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56681" type="x-p"/> 7. The rabbins say, that "God gave to the Israelites a sword, on which the ineffable name יהוה Yehovah was inscribed; and as long as they held that sword the angel of death had no power over them." Shemoth Rabba, sec. 51, fol. 143, 2. Bemidbar Rabba, sec. 12, fol. 214, 2. <div eID="gen56681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56682" type="x-p"/> In the latter tract, sec. 16, fol. 232, 3, and in Rab. Tanchum, fol. 66, mention is made of the guardian angels of the Israelites, who were clothed with purple vestments, on which was inscribed שם המפורש shem hammephorash, the ineffable name. See more in Schoettgen. <div eID="gen56682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56683" type="x-p"/> 8. But what comes nearer to the point, in reference to the title given here to Christ, is what is related of Sesostris by Diodorus Siculus, lib. i. c. 55, p. 166, edit. Bipont, of whom he says: "Having pushed his conquests as far as Thrace, he erected pillars, on which were the following words in Egyptian hieroglyphics: Τηνδε την χωραν ὁπλοις κατεστρεψατο τοις ἑαυτου Βασιλευς Βασιλεων, και Δεσποτης Δεσποτων, Σεσοωσις·" This province, Sesoosis, (Sesostris), King of Kings and Lord of Lords, conquered by his own arms. This inscription is conceived almost in the words of St. John. Now the Greek historian did not borrow the words from the apostle, as he died in the reign of Augustus, about the time of our Lord's incarnation. This cannot be the same inscription mentioned above by Herodotus, the one being in Ionia, the other in Thrace: but as he erected several of those pillars or images, probably a nearly similar inscription was found on each. <div eID="gen56683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56684" type="x-p"/> 9. This custom seems to have been common among the ancient Egyptians. Inscriptions are frequently found on the images of Isis, Osiris, Anubis, etc., at the feet, on the head, on the back, on the girdle, etc., etc. Eight of those ancient images in my own collection abound with these inscriptions. <div eID="gen56684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56685" type="x-p"/> 1. Osiris, four inches and a quarter high, standing on a thrones all covered over with hieroglyphics exquisitely engraved. <div eID="gen56685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56686" type="x-p"/> 2. Anubis, six inches high, with a tiara, on the back of which is cut ΛΕΓΟΡΝΥΘ , in uncial Greek characters. <div eID="gen56686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56687" type="x-p"/> 3. The Cercopithecus, seven inches long, sitting on a pedestal, and at his feet, in the same characters, ΧΑΔΕΟ. <div eID="gen56687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56688" type="x-p"/> 4. An Isis, about eight inches high, on her back ΔΡΥΓΟ. <div eID="gen56688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56689" type="x-p"/> 5. Ditto, seven inches, beautifully cut, standing, holding a serpent in her left hand, and at her feet ΕΤΑΠΥΓΙ. <div eID="gen56689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56690" type="x-p"/> 6. Ditto, five inches and a quarter, round whose girdle is ΠΙΕΥΧΥΔΙ; but part of this inscription appears to be hidden under her arms, which are extended by her side. <div eID="gen56690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56691" type="x-p"/> 7. Ditto, five inches high, hooded, with a loose stola, down the back of which are seven lines of Greek uncial characters, but nearly obliterated. <div eID="gen56691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56692" type="x-p"/> 8. Ditto, four inches high, with a girdle going round the back immediately under the arms, the front of which is hidden under a sort of a stomacher; on the part that appears are these characters, ΧΕΝΛΑ. These may be all intended as a kind of abrasaxas or tutelary deities; and I give this notice of them, and the inscriptions upon them, partly in illustration of the text, and partly to engage my learned and antiquarian readers in attempts to decipher them. I would have given the Etruscan characters on the other images described above, but have no method of imitating them except by an engraving. <div eID="gen56692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56693" type="x-p"/> As these kinds of inscriptions on the thigh, the garments, and different parts of the body, were in use among different nations, to express character, conduct, qualities, and conquests, we may rest assured that to them St. John alludes when he represents our sovereign Lord with an inscription upon his vesture and upon his thigh; and had we not found it a custom among other nations, we should have been at a loss to account for its introduction and meaning here.
entries.7f0f4be2ce8cef9b391a7f21fbf3b8c0471987dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen56693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56694" type="x-p"/> An angel standing in the sun - Exceedingly luminous; every part of him emitting rays of light. From this representation, Milton has taken his description of Uriel, the angel of the sun. Paradise Lost, b. iii. l. 648 - "The Archangel Uriel, one of the seven Who, in God's presence, nearest to his throne Stands ready at command and are his eyes That run through all the heavens, or down to the earth Bears his swift errands over moist and dry, Over sea and land." <div eID="gen56694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56695" type="x-p"/> All the fowls that fly - The carcasses of God's enemies shall be food for all the fowls of heaven. This is according to a Jewish tradition, Synopsis Sohar, p. 114, n. 25: "In the time when God shall execute vengeance for the people of Israel, he shall feed all the beasts of the earth for twelve months with their flesh and all the fowls for seven years." It is well known that both beasts and birds of prey are accustomed to frequent fields of battle, and live upon the slain.
entries.9961e1b0ad63d6014c7ae4fcdc77fa327b7f264f: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen56695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56696" type="x-p"/> That ye may eat the flesh of kings - There shall be a universal destruction; the kings, generals, captains, and all their host, shall be slain.
entries.9f869686c91d59257f9aca04d62f0fe649fd8a2c: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen56696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56697" type="x-p"/> I saw the beast - See the notes on Revelation 12 (note), Revelation 13 (note) and Revelation 17 (note).
entries.bab63273a5b41e0c4a61ece48ee90a7b3af9b107: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen56697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56698" type="x-p"/> And the beast was taken, and - the false prophet - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Rev.17.8">Rev 17:8</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen56698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56699" type="x-p"/> That worshipped his image - The beast has been represented as the Latin empire; the image of the beast, the popes of Rome; and the false prophet, the papal clergy. <div eID="gen56699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56700" type="x-p"/> Were cast alive into a lake of fire - Were discomfited when alive - in the zenith of their power, and destroyed with an utter destruction.
entries.132cd5baa2a785f2b55f02e7998a9c5ce22215cd: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen56700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56701" type="x-p"/> With the sword of him that sat upon the horse - He who sat on the white horse is Christ; and his sword is his word - the unadulterated Gospel.  <chapter eID="Rev.19"/> <div eID="gen56701" type="x-p"/>

entries.aa296d8fe295f554a9cbbe582729d7a9ca2b9634:
CHAPTER XIX

ANALYSIS OF THE CHAPTER

THIS chapter, as well as the last, is an episode, delaying the final catastrophe, and describing more fully the effect of the destruction of the mystical Babylon. The chapter consists of the following parts:--

I. A hymn of the heavenly hosts in view of the destruction of the mystical Babylon, Rev 19:1-7.

(a) A voice is heard in heaven shouting Hallelujah, in view of the fact that God had judged the great harlot that had corrupted the earth, Rev 19:1,2.

(b) The sound is echoed and repeated as the smoke of her torment ascends, Rev 19:3.

(c) The four and twenty elders, and the four living creatures, as interested in all that pertains to the church, unite in that shout of Hallelujah, Rev 19:4.

(d) A voice is heard from the throne commanding them to praise God, Rev 19:5; and

(e) the mighty shout of Hallelujah is echoed and repeated from unnumbered hosts, Rev 19:6,7.

II. The marriage of the Lamb, Rev 19:8,9. The Lamb of God is united to his bride--the church--never more to be separated; and after all the persecutions, conflicts, and embarrassments which had existed, this long-desired union is consummated, and the glorious triumph of the church is described under the image of a joyous wedding ceremony.

III. John is so overcome with this representation, that in his transports of feeling he prostrates himself before the angel, who shows him all this, ready to worship one who discloses such bright and glorious scenes, Rev 19:10. He is gently rebuked for allowing himself to be so overcome that he would render Divine homage to any creature, and is told that he who communicates this to him is but a fellow-servant, and that God only is to be worshipped.

IV. The final conquest over the beast and the false prophet, and the subjugation of all the foes of the church, Rev 9:11-21.

(a) A description of the conqueror--the Son of God, Rev 9:11-16. He appears on a white horse--emblem of victory. He has on his head many crowns; wears a vesture dipped in blood; is followed by the armies of heaven on white horses; from his mouth goes a sharp sword; and his name is prominently written on his vesture and his thigh--all emblematic of certain victory.

(b) An angel is seen standing in the sun, calling on all the fowls of heaven to come to the great feast prepared for them in the destruction of the enemies of God--as if there were a great slaughter sufficient to supply all the fowls that feed on flesh, Rev 19:17,18.

(c) The final war, Rev 19:19,21. The beast, and the kings of the earth, and their armies are gathered together for battle; the beast and the false prophet are taken, and are cast into the lake that burns with fire and brimstone; and all that remain of the enemies of God are slain, and the fowls are satisfied with their flesh. The last obstacle that prevented the dawn of the millennial morning is taken away, and the church is triumphant.

Verse 1. And after these things. The things particularly that were exhibited in the previous chapter. Rev 18:1.

I heard a voice of much people in heaven. The voice of the worshippers before the throne.

Saying, Alleluia. The Greek method of writing Hallelujah. This word--αλληλουια--occurs in the New Testament only in this chapter, Rev 18:1,3,4,6. The Hebrew phrase-- ? Hallelujah--occurs often in the Old Testament. It means properly Praise Jehovah, or Praise the Lord. The occasion on which it is introduced here is very appropriate. It is uttered by the inhabitants of heaven, in the immediate presence of God himself, and in view of the final overthrow of the enemies of the church and the triumph of the gospel. In such circumstances it was fit that heaven should render praise, and that a song of thanksgiving should be uttered in which all holy beings could unite.

Salvation. That is, the salvation is to be ascribed to God. Rev 7:10.

And glory, and honour. Barnes on "Re 5:12".

And power. Rev 5:13.

Unto the Lord our God. That is, all that there is of honour, glory, power, in the redemption of the world belongs to God, and should be ascribed to him. This is expressive of the true feelings of piety always; this will constitute the song of heaven.
